results.title: Repdigits with repdigit digital product are repunits from a(16) = 1111 on (A201060)
results.summary: Let a(1) < a(2) < ... list the repdigits (all decimal digits equal; 0 counts) whose digital product is also a repdigit. Then a(n) is a repunit (all digits equal to 1) for every n >= 16. Formally: forall n >= 16, IsRepunit (a n), where a n = Nat.nth IsTerm (n - 1).
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: "Conjecture: a(n) is repunit for n >= 16." (A201060, entry by _Jaroslav Krizek_, Nov 26 2011)

Referees: Main citations:
- R. Obláth, "Une propriété des puissances parfaites", Mathesis 65 (1956), 356–364. It shows that the only perfect powers with all decimal digits equal to some a != 1 are 4, 8 and 9.
- Y. Bugeaud and M. Mignotte, "On integers with identical digits", Mathematika 46 (1999), 411–417. It shows that no decimal repunit with two or more digits is a perfect power.
Together these say that no repdigit >= 10 is a perfect power, and the A201060 conjecture follows directly, since d^k >= 16 for 2 <= d <= 9 and k >= 4.

Both results are restated in O. Kihel and F. Luca, "Perfect Powers With All Equal Digits But One", J. Integer Seq. 8 (2005), Article 05.5.7, Introduction (https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL8/Kihel/kihel7.html). See also A. Gica and L. Panaitopol, "On Oblath's Problem", J. Integer Seq. 6 (2003), Article 03.3.5, which is linked from OEIS A018885 and A368049. The Wikipedia article "Repdigit" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Repdigit) covers the related Nagell–Ljunggren equation and cites Bugeaud–Mignotte 2002.

The OEIS entry A201060 (local mirror, revision #11, 2012) still labels the statement as a conjecture, and I found no web or arXiv discussion that names A201060.

results.title: Positivity of the exponential Mertens function (A209802)
results.summary: Let mu_e be the exponential Möbius function (A166234). It is multiplicative with mu_e(p^e) = mu(e), so mu_e(n) = prod_{p | n} mu(v_p(n)). Let a(n) = sum_{k=1}^{n} mu_e(k) (A209802). Then a(n) > 0 for every n >= 1. This is Zumkeller's conjecture in the OEIS entry.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: A209802 (Partial sums of exponential Möbius function, A166234): "Analog of Mertens's function, A002321; conjecture: a(n) > 0." (entry by _Reinhard Zumkeller_, Mar 13 2012)

Referees: No explicit resolution of the A209802 conjecture found:
- OEIS A209802 (https://oeis.org/A209802) and its history (https://oeis.org/history?seq=A209802, versions 1-29) still list "conjecture: a(n) > 0"; nothing about a proof is recorded.
- A166234 (exponential Möbius function) and A368405 add nothing on positivity.

Prior results that imply the conjecture at once:
- K. Rogers, "The Schnirelmann density of the squarefree integers", Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. 15 (1964) 515-516, doi:10.1090/S0002-9939-1964-0163893-X. It proves Q(n) >= 53n/88 for all n, with equality only at n = 176.
- L. Moser and R. A. MacLeod, "The error term for the squarefree integers", Canad. Math. Bull. 9 (1966), doi:10.4153/CMB-1966-039-4.
- The same bound is recorded in an OEIS A013928 comment (M. Marcus 2012; C. R. Greathouse IV 2016).
- L. Tóth, "On certain arithmetic functions involving exponential divisors, II", Annales Univ. Sci. Budapest. Sect. Comp. 27 (2007) 155-166, arXiv:0708.3557. It gives mu_e taking values in {-1, 0, 1} with mu_e(p) = 1, and the asymptotic sum mu_e(n) = c x + O(x^{1/2} log x) with c about 0.36094. That settles positivity only for large x.

Together these give a(n) >= 2Q(n) - n >= 9n/44 > 0 for all n >= 1.

Also checked, with nothing relevant found:
- Lelechenko, arXiv:1405.7597
- Cao and Zhai, J. Integer Seq. 13 (2010)
- Web, MathOverflow and Math StackExchange searches

results.title: An equiangular decagon with sides in arithmetic progression (A215010)
results.summary: Garcia's conjecture (OEIS A215010) says that hexagons are the only equiangular simple convex polygons whose integer side lengths are the N terms t, t+d, ..., t+(N-1)d (with d ≥ 1) of an arithmetic progression, in some order. Formally: if N ≥ 3, every side t + σ(k)·d is positive, and Σ_k (t + σ(k)d)·exp(2πik/N) = 0 for a permutation σ of Fin N, then N = 6. We prove that this is false. Take N = 10 and t = d = 1, with consecutive sides (1, 4, 5, 8, 9, 2, 3, 6, 7, 10), so σ = (0, 3, 4, 7, 8, 1, 2, 5, 6, 9). This gives an equiangular decagon.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: "Conjecture: hexagons are the only simple convex polygons with equal interior angles with such property, due to the fact that cos(Pi/3) = 1/2." Here 'such property' means integer side lengths in arithmetic progression t+m*d, as in the entry name. (entry by _Robin Garcia_, Jul 31 2012)

Referees: Prior refutations, all at least as old as or published soon after Garcia's 2012 conjecture:

(1) OEIS A118887 (H. Pfoertner, May 03 2006). "Number of ways to place n objects with weights 1,...,n evenly spaced around a circle so it balances." T. D. Noe, Sep 13 2005: "Also number of equiangular polygons whose sides are some permutation of 1,2,3,...,n." The data have included a(10)=24, a(12)=732, a(14)=720, a(15)=48 since the first revision in 2006. W. Edwin Clark (Sep 14 2005) proved there are no solutions when n is a prime power. J. Sondow (Oct 17 2013) records that Murray Klamkin proved solutions exist when n is not a prime power, and adds the formula a(A024619(n)) > 0. The problem was proposed by Brendan McKay on the SeqFan mailing list, Sep 12 2005. https://oeis.org/A118887

(2) G. J. Woeginger, "Nothing new about equiangular polygons", Amer. Math. Monthly 120(9) (2013) 849–850, doi:10.4169/amer.math.monthly.120.09.849. Abstract: "We survey results on equiangular n-vertex polygons with edge lengths in arithmetic progression. Such a polygon exists if and only if n has at least two distinct prime factors." This is exactly the A215010 setting, and it gives n = 10, 12, 14, 15, ... as counterexamples.

(3) Supporting references:
- D. Ball, "Equiangular polygons", Math. Gazette 86 (2002) 396–407.
- A. Bernoff, "Bernoff's Puzzler", MuddMath Newsletter 4(1) (2005), p. 10.
- M. Munteanu and L. Munteanu, "Rational equiangular polygons", Applied Math. 4 (2013) 1460–1465, doi:10.4236/am.2013.410197.
- U. Abel, "Coincidence of the barycentre and the geometric centre of weighted points", Math. Gazette (online Oct 2019). It restates the criterion: at least two distinct prime factors.

A215010 itself (history checked through revision #43, Jan 23 2015) never cites any of these, and its conjecture remains uncorrected. I found no earlier formalization in Lean or any other proof assistant.

results.title: Every odd prime is a side of a Heronian triangle (A229159)
results.summary: For every prime p > 2 there are natural numbers x, y, z, A such that x, y, z satisfy the strict triangle inequalities (x < y + z, y < x + z, z < x + y), Heron's formula 16 A^2 = (x+y+z)(-x+y+z)(x-y+z)(x+y-z) holds in Z, and at least one of x, y, z equals p.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: "Conjecture: for all prime p > 2 there exists an integer-sided triangle with integer area where at least one side is of length p." (entry by _Michel Lagneau_, Sep 17 2013)

Referees: Classical formula (n, (n^2-1)/2, (n^2+1)/2) for odd n, credited to the Pythagoreans (Proclus, Commentary on Euclid's Elements I.47; H. Eves, An Introduction to the History of Mathematics, sec. 3-4; cf. Euclid, Elements X, Lemma 1 before Prop. 29). OEIS A046079, comment by Richard R. Forberg, May 31 2013: "For odd n: L = (n^2-1)/2 and H = L+1". In the same entry, Ant King (Jan 29 2011) notes that for n > 2 the n with exactly one Pythagorean triangle on leg n are the primes and their doubles. OEIS A042965 (Sloane, May 30 2014): the primes that are a difference of two squares are exactly the odd primes. Related: A009004 (short legs of Pythagorean triangles). Mathlib has the Pythagorean triple classification (Mathlib/NumberTheory/PythagoreanTriples.lean) but not this Heronian statement. I found no source that addresses A229159's conjecture directly; it is resolved immediately by the classical formula.

results.title: A262957: Israel's b(n), c(n) are coprime integers and a(n) = b(n)
results.summary: Let cf(n) be the value of 1 - 1/(2 + 1/(3 - 1/(4 + ... (n+1) + (-1)^(n+1)/1))), where the integers 1, ..., n+1 are used, the sign after k is (-1)^k, and the innermost tail is 1. Let a(n) be the numerator of cf(n) in lowest terms. Robert Israel defined b and c by b(1)=2, b(2)=3, c(1)=3, c(2)=5 and, for both, x(n+1) = (((-1)^n(n-1) + n(n+2)) x(n) - (1 + (-1)^n(n+1)) x(n-1)) / (n - (-1)^n). Claim (Israel's conjecture, OEIS A262957): for every n >= 1, b(n) and c(n) are integers with gcd(b(n), c(n)) = 1, and a(n) = b(n).
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: Conjecture: b(n) and c(n) are coprime for all n, so that a(n) = b(n). I have verified this for n <= 10000. - _Robert Israel_, Dec 22 2015 [b(1)=2, b(2)=3, c(1)=3, c(2)=5, b(n+1) = (((-1)^n*(n-1)+n*(n+2))*b(n) - (1+(-1)^n*(n+1))*b(n-1))/(n-(-1)^n), same recurrence for c]

Referees: OEIS A262957 (local mirror, rev #80, Mar 2025): Robert Israel's comment of Dec 22 2015 states the conjecture, verified for n <= 10000, and it is still listed as open. Peter Bala, "A note on A262957 and A263295" (Dec 24 2015, linked from the OEIS entry): proves the simple continued fraction expansion [0;1,1,2,1,3,4,1,5,6,...] of the limit, but not Israel's recurrence or the coprimality. The cross-referenced entries A263295, A346590, A244279 and A244280 contain no proof. A262957 is absent from Tom Adamczewski, "OEIS Open: How many conjectures can language models turn into theorems?", arXiv:2608.11941 (2026), and from the epoch-research/LeanOpenProblems and LeanOpenProblems-results repositories. Web searches of arXiv, MathOverflow, Math StackExchange and SeqFan found no prior resolution. The proof uses the classical determinant identity for continued-fraction convergents (p_{k+1}q_k - p_k q_{k+1} = ±1).

results.title: Lang's conjecture a(n) = A250400(n+1)/(n+1) for A294512 fails at n = 164
results.summary: Let V(n) = sum_{k=0}^{n} 1/((k+1)(3k+1)) and let a(n) be the denominator of V(n) in lowest terms (OEIS A294512). Let A250400(m) be the numerator, in lowest terms, of the harmonic mean m / sum_{j=1}^{m} 1/(j(3j-2)) of the first m octagonal numbers. results.title: Domino-tileable Young diagrams are exactly the colour-balanced ones (A300789)
results.summary: For every integer partition y = (y_1 >= y_2 >= ... >= y_m), the Young diagram of y can be tiled by dominoes if and only if the number of odd parts in even positions equals the number of odd parts in odd positions. So the Heinz numbers of domino-tileable partitions (A300789) are exactly the Heinz numbers of partitions whose odd parts appear as often in even as in odd positions. Equivalently, a(n) = b(n) for all n >= 1, where a(n) and b(n) are the n-th smallest Heinz numbers of the two classes.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: %C A300789 This sequence is conjectured to be the Heinz numbers of integer partitions in which the odd parts appear as many times in even as in odd positions.  (_Gus Wiseman_, Mar 12 2018)

Referees: Already known, so the Lean proof is a first formalization, not a new result:
- Classical 2-core / beta-number theory. I.G. Macdonald, Symmetric Functions and Hall Polynomials (2nd ed. 1995), Ch. I §1 Ex. 8, pp. 12-15: the r-core is empty iff the beta-numbers are equidistributed mod r. D.E. Littlewood, Modular representations of symmetric groups, Proc. Roy. Soc. A 209 (1951) 333-353.
- Explicit statement of the parity form. S.P. Albion, "Proof of some Littlewood identities conjectured by Lee, Rains and Warnaar", arXiv:2108.12766, Lemma 2.1: empty 2-core (i.e. domino-tileable) iff {lambda_i + 2n - i} has n even and n odd elements, which is equivalent to the A300789 parity condition.
- Black = white criterion for Young diagrams. Codeforces Round 609 editorial, problem 1268B/1269D "Domino for Young" (Dec 2019, codeforces.com/blog/entry/72358).

results.title: Perimeters of primitive Heronian isosceles triangles: A308222(n) = 2 · A096033(n + 2)
results.summary: Let a(n) be the n-th smallest perimeter of a primitive Heronian isosceles triangle (integer sides with no common divisor, integer area, two sides equal). Let A096033(n) be the n-th smallest difference z - x, where x is a leg and z the hypotenuse of a primitive Pythagorean triangle. Then for every n ≥ 1, a(n) = 2 · A096033(n + 2).
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: %F a(n) = 2*A096033(n+2) (conjectured). (Peter Kagey, May 16 2019)

Referees: Main prior resolution: Math StackExchange answer 3230072 by user "George", 2019-05-17 (https://math.stackexchange.com/a/3230072), answering Peter Kagey's question 3230019, "Semiperimeter of isosceles Heronian triangles". It is linked in the A308222 %H line. It derives that primitive isosceles Heronian triangles are (u^2+v^2, u^2+v^2, 2(u^2-v^2)) or (u^2+v^2, u^2+v^2, 4uv) with semiperimeters 2u^2 or (u+v)^2, citing J. R. Carlson, "Determination of Heronian Triangles", Fibonacci Quarterly 8 (1970) 499-506, Lemma 2.

results.title: Fixed polyominoes with n cells and width n-2: T(n,n-2) = 8n^2 - 51n + 86 (A308359)
results.summary: For every n >= 5, the number T(n, n-2) of fixed polyominoes with n cells whose convex hull has width n-2 equals 8n^2 - 51n + 86. A fixed polyomino is a finite edge-connected set of grid cells, taken up to translation. The statement file encodes it as the normalized set S in N x N that has min x = 0 and min y = 0. The height is unrestricted.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: %F A308359 Conjecture: T(n,n-2) = 8*n^2 - 51*n + 86 for n >= 5.  (Entry by _R. J. Mathar_, May 22 2019; last edit Oct 10 2022.)

Referees: A. Goupil, H. Cloutier, F. Nouboud, "Enumeration of inscribed polyominos", FPSAC 2010, DMTCS proc. AN (2010) 737-748 (https://dmtcs.episciences.org/2808; hal-01186234; cited in OEIS A196593). Theorem 1 gives pmin(b,k) = 2k+2b-3bk-8+8*C(b+k-2,b-1), so pmin(w,3) = 4w^2-3w-2. Theorem 3 (k=2, b>2) gives pmin+1(b,2) = 4b^2-16b+18. Since T(n,n-2) = pmin(n-2,3) + pmin+1(n-2,2) = 8(n-2)^2-19(n-2)+16 = 8n^2-51n+86, Mathar's 2019 conjecture follows directly. The OEIS A308359 entry (last edited Oct 2022) still says "Conjecture" and has no proof note. Related but not resolving: L. Marin, "Counting Polyominoes in a Rectangle b x h", arXiv:2406.16413 (EPTCS 403, 2024), which covers fixed width and any height. I found no MathOverflow, Math StackExchange or SeqFan discussion explicitly proving the A308359 formula.

results.title: Odd terms of A323695 occur only at n = k(k+2)
results.summary: Let a(N) be the coefficient of x^N in Sum_{m>=0} x^m (1 - x^(m+1))^m / (1 + x^(m+1))^(m+1) (OEIS A323695, offset 0). If a(n) is odd, then n = k(k+2) for some natural number k. Equivalently, if a(n) is odd then n + 1 is a perfect square.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: A323695 (G.f.: Sum_{n>=0} x^n (1 - x^(n+1))^n/(1 + x^(n+1))^(n+1)): "Odd terms occur only at n = k*(k+2) for k >= 0 (conjecture);" (_Paul D. Hanna_, Feb 23 2019). A324300 (G.f.: Sum_{n>=0} x^n (x^(n+1)+i)^n/(1 + i x^(n+1))^(n+1)): "Odd terms occur only at n = k*(k+2) for k >= 0 (conjecture);" (Hanna, Feb 21 2019).

Referees: OEIS A323695 (Hanna, Feb 23 2019; still labeled "(conjecture)" at rev #24, Dec 15 2024; history checked) and its cross-references A323696, A324300 (same conjecture for an i-variant, also unproved), A323675 and A323680. Sibling results proved by others, which do not cover A323695: A325046, odd terms iff N = m(m+1), in S. Fried, "Further proofs of conjectures from the OEIS", arXiv:2607.24832 (Thm 50), also in google-deepmind/alphaproof-nexus-results; A323557, odd terms at r(r+1), in T. Adamczewski, "OEIS Open", arXiv:2608.11941 and AlphaProof Nexus (Tsoukalas et al.). A323695 is in neither google-deepmind/formal-conjectures nor epoch-research/LeanOpenProblems. results.title: Prime-Minesweeper on the A060734 array: a(n) < 6, and a(n) = 5 only at n = 6
results.summary: Write the positive integers into the square array A060734. The cell in row r, column c (both counted from 0) holds val(r,c) = (c+1)^2 - r if r <= c, and r^2 + 1 + c if r > c. Every positive integer appears in exactly one cell. Set a(n) = -1 if n is prime. Otherwise a(n) is the number of primes in the king-move neighbouring cells of n's cell. There are up to 8 such cells, 5 on row 0 or column 0, and 3 at the corner (0,0). Claim: for every n >= 1 we have a(n) < 6, and a(n) = 5 holds exactly when n = 6.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: %C a(n) < 6 (conjectured). %C a(n) = 5 for n={6} (conjectured). %C Set of n such that a(n) = 4 is unbounded (conjectured). (Witold Tatkiewicz, Oct 02 2019)

Referees: OEIS A326407 (Tatkiewicz, Oct 2019; last edit #27, Mar 20 2020) still lists "a(n) < 6" and "a(n) = 5 for n={6}" as conjectured, with no %E edits or proof links. OEIS A327893 (hexagonal spiral, De Vlieger 2019) records Tatkiewicz's parity argument bounding its terms by 4. That is the same technique applied to a different grid, not a proof for A326407. OEIS A326408 and A326409 state "a(n) < 5" without "(conjectured)" but give no proof. A326405, A326406, A326410, A060734, A136626 and A136627 contain nothing relevant. Web searches (arXiv, MathOverflow/Math StackExchange, SeqFan, general) found no prior proof or counterexample for A326407.

results.title: A326602: a(n) is odd iff n is a square
results.summary: Let A(x) = Sum_{n>=0} (x^(2n-1)+1)^n x^n / (1+x^(2n+1))^(n+1) in Z[[x]] (the n=0 summand is 1/(1+x)), and let a(n) = [x^(2n)] A(x). Then for every n >= 0, a(n) is odd if and only if n is a perfect square (n = k^2 for some k >= 0, so 0 counts as a square).
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: A326602 (G.f.: Sum_{n>=0} (x^(2n-1)+1)^n x^n/(1+x^(2n+1))^(n+1), an even function; a(n) = [x^(2n)]): "a(n) is odd iff n is square (conjecture)." (_Paul D. Hanna_, Aug 08 2019). Same family: A323689 (Sum (x^n+i)^n/(1+i x^n)^(n+1)): "Odd terms occur only at n = k^2 for k >= 0 (conjecture);" (Hanna, Feb 14 2019); A323675 (Sum x^n (x^n+i)^n/(1+i x^(n+1))^(n+1)): "It appears that odd terms occur only at n*(n+1)" (Hanna, Feb 10 2019); A323690 (Sum (x^(n+1)+i)^n/(1+i x^n)^(n+1)): "the first column consists of all the odd terms" (triangle rows start at n(n+1)) (Hanna, Feb 13 2019).

Referees: No prior resolution of A326602 found.

results.title: A332010: the average first letter of one-descent derangements has denominator 2^(n-2)
results.summary: For every n ≥ 2, take the derangements of {1, ..., n} (in one-line notation) that have exactly one descent. The average of their first letters, written in lowest terms, has denominator 2^(n-2). This is Kagey's conjecture T(n,1) = 2^(n-2) in OEIS A332010.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: "Conjecture: T(n, 1) = 2^(n-2)." (A332010, entry by Peter Kagey, Feb 04 2020)

Referees: No prior resolution found.
- OEIS A332010 and A332009 (Peter Kagey, Feb 04 2020; last edits Mar 30 2024) still state "Conjecture: T(n,1) = 2^(n-2)" and "Conjecture: T(n,1) = A083329(n-1)", with no proof recorded in comments or %E lines. I checked both the local mirror and raw.githubusercontent oeisdata.
- Related known facts:
  - A219836 (Callan 2012; links to Fu–Lin–Zeng arXiv:1507.05184 and Alexandersson arXiv:2609.07325) gives a recurrence implying there are 2^(n-2) derangements with one descent. That is only the unreduced denominator.

results.title: The period of 1/11^n is 2 * 11^(n-1)
results.summary: For every n >= 1, the period of the decimal expansion of 1/11^n is 2 * 11^(n-1). Equivalently, the multiplicative order of 10 modulo 11^n is 2 * 11^(n-1). This is the FORMULA conjecture of OEIS A334603.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: Comment: "Conjecture proposed by the authors in References page 205: if p is a prime with gcd(p,30) = 1 and if the period of 1/p is m then the period of 1/p^n is m*p^(n-1)." Formula: "a(n) = 2 * 11^(n-1) [conjectured, see comments]." (_Bernard Schott_, May 07 2020)

Referees: The result is classical; no formalization of this specific statement was found.

Classical theory: Gauss, Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (1801), on orders modulo p^n and on periods of decimal fractions with prime-power denominators (Arts. 85-89, 312-318). Standard elementary number theory texts (Ireland-Rosen; Niven-Zuckerman-Montgomery) state the lifting lemma: if p is odd and a^{ord_p a} = 1 + p*c with p ∤ c, then ord_{p^n}(a) = p^{n-1} * ord_p(a). Mathlib's ZMod.orderOf_one_add_mul_prime is that lemma for 1 + p*a.

Explicit decimal-period statements:
- K. A. Ross, "Repeating Decimals: A Period Piece", Mathematics Magazine 83 (2010), 33-45. If n is the largest exponent with period(1/p^n) = period(1/p), then period(1/p^a) = period(1/p) * p^(a-n) for a > n. For p = 11, period(1/121) = 22 ≠ 2, so n = 1.
- S. Yao and A. Toyohara, "The length of the repeating decimal", arXiv:2507.01295 (2025), Theorem 2.1: l_{p^n} = p^{n-(m_p+1)} * l_p, where m_p = v_p((10^{l_p} - 1)/p). For p = 11 this gives m = v_11(9) = 0, so l_{11^n} = 2*11^(n-1).
- Wikipedia, "Repeating decimal": the period of 1/p^2 is usually p*T_p, with the only known exceptions 3, 487 and 56598313.
- OEIS A045616 (primes with 10^(p-1) ≡ 1 mod p^2) lists exactly these exceptions, and 11 is not among them.
- John D. Cook, "Reciprocals of prime powers" (blog, 2021-09-28) checks 1/121 explicitly: period 22.

In the OEIS itself, A055272 has a Sep 2026 comment by E. Rodríguez proving the analogous 7^n case with the same lifting argument.

Side note: the general conjecture of De Koninck and Mercier quoted in the A334603 comments (not the formalized statement) is false at p = 487.

Sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.01295 ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Repeating_decimal ; https://www.johndcook.com/blog/2021/09/28/reciprocals-of-prime-powers/ ; https://oeis.org/A045616 (read from the local mirror)

results.title: Repunit residues: a(n) = n - 1 exactly for long period primes
results.summary: For n >= 1 let a(n) be the number of distinct values R_k mod n for 1 <= k <= n, where R_k = (10^k - 1)/9 is the k-th repunit. Then a(n) = n - 1 if and only if n is a long period prime (A006883): n is prime and either n = 2 or the multiplicative order of 10 modulo n is n - 1.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: Conjecture: a(n) = n-1 if and only if n is a long period prime (A006883), that is, n is a prime and the decimal expansion of 1/n has period n-1. (entry by _Sen-Peng Eu_, May 19 2020)

Referees: OEIS A335012 (Sen-Peng Eu, May 19 2020): the current revision #31 (Mar 12 2026) still lists this as a conjecture, with no %E line recording a resolution. In the same entry, Robert Israel's comment (Jun 25 2020) gives a(n) = A084680(n), the order of 10 mod n, when gcd(n,30) = 1. That implicitly settles the coprime-to-30 case but not n divisible by 2, 3 or 5. Cross-references: A006883 (long period primes, including 2) and A084680; neither mentions a proof. Background only: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Repunit (pigeonhole argument that some repunit is a multiple of n; R_k ≡ k mod 3), https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Full_reptend_prime, https://mathworld.wolfram.com/FullReptendPrime.html. Web searches of arXiv, MathOverflow, Math StackExchange, SeqFan and the Google index found no earlier proof or counterexample.

results.title: A338885: the smallest number in row 655 is 104, not A228286(655) = 115
results.summary: Kagey's conjecture in OEIS A338885 says that for every n ≥ 2, the smallest k for which a diagonal lattice rectangle (integer vertices, no side parallel to the x-axis) lies in the n X k box [0,n]×[0,k] and touches all four of its sides is A228286(n) = min{x + y*z : x, y, z ≥ 1, x*y + z = n}. This is false. For n = 655, the value k = 104 is in the row, but A228286(655) = 115 ≥ 105. So A228286(655) is not the least element of row 655.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: "Conjecture: The smallest number in the n-th row is A228286(n)." (entry by _Peter Kagey_, Nov 14 2020; a second conjecture in the same entry, "The largest number in the n-th row is A033638(n)", is true; see approach)

Referees: I found no prior resolution.
- OEIS A338885 (Kagey, Nov 14 2020): I checked both the local mirror and the latest raw oeisdata version (rev #22, Sep 11 2021). The conjecture is still listed, with no counterexample noted, and the b-file covers only rows 2..101.
- Cross-references (local mirror): A228286, A228287, A228288, A338886, A338887, A033638, A085582, A113751. None of them mentions a resolution.
- Code Golf SE question 213754 "Rectangles in rectangles", read via the Stack Exchange API: neither the answers nor the comments mention the conjecture.
- Web searches (OEIS/A338885, Kagey, SeqFan, the min x+yz / ab+cd formulations, ARML 2013) turned up nothing relevant.
- Independent computation: n = 655 is the smallest counterexample (row min 104 vs A228286 = 115). Further counterexamples are at n = 845, 909 and 1019 for n <= 1200.

results.title: Every n not divisible by 5 has a multiple with only prime digits (A342992)
results.summary: For every integer n >= 1 with 5 not dividing n, there is some k such that k*n is positive and every decimal digit of k*n is prime (in {2,3,5,7}). Equivalently, a(n) > 0 for A342992 (Sariyar's conjecture).
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: "Conjecture: a(n) > 0 for all n that are not divisible by 5." (A342992, entry by _Metin Sariyar_, Apr 13 2021. Corneth added that a(625k) = 0.)

Referees: No prior explicit proof of the A342992 conjecture was found. The entry still lists it as a conjecture (#60, Apr 22 2021) with no later %E edits.

Closest prior material:
(1) OEIS A078239 (Murthy 2002; Robert Israel, Feb 2018). Comment: "Besides multiples of 10, 625 and its odd multiples have a(n)=0". Its Maple program implicitly assumes a prime-digit multiple exists for every n with 10∤n and 625∤n. This is an unproved assertion. A078250 (Howroyd, 2024) repeats the comment.
(2) OEIS A053316 (Henry Bottomley, Mar 2000; formula corrected by Israel, 2019): an n-digit number with digits 2 and 3 that is divisible by 2^n. This is exactly the proof's block lemma. The digits-{1,2} version is A053312, the 1971 All-Union olympiad problem (cut-the-knot.org/arithmetic/DivisibilityFromSovietMO.shtml).
(3) IMO Shortlist 1994 N7, "wobbly numbers" (prase.cz/kalva/short/soln/sh94n7.html): the same technique of combining a 2-power block with the coprime-to-10 part by repetition.
(4) Galperin & Reid, "Multiples Without Large Digits", Amer. Math. Monthly 126 (2019), as cited by John D. Cook (johndcook.com/blog/2025/12/16/multiples-with-no-large-digits/), with the citation's page numbers disputed by a reader comment. It covers digits 1–5 and does not imply this result.
(5) C. W. Wu, "Pigeonholes and repunits", Amer. Math. Monthly 121 (2014): the related {0,1} case.

The result is elementary and folklore-adjacent, but no source states or proves it for prime digits or for digits {2,3}.

results.title: A344710: non-obtuse lattice triangles with sides >= sqrt(n) have |det| > (sqrt 3 / 2) n
results.summary: For every n >= 1, let a(n) be the least value of |det(B-A, C-A)| (twice the area) over lattice triangles ABC in Z^2 that are non-degenerate and non-obtuse and have all three squared side lengths >= n. Then sqrt(3/4) * n < a(n). This is Waldmann's conjectured inequality in OEIS A344710.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: Formula: "a(n) > sqrt(3/4)*n (conjectured)." Comment: "Conjectured next terms (from the conjectured inequality a(n) > sqrt(3/4)*n) are a(50,...,64) ?= 45, 48, 48, 52, 55, 55, 55, 55, 55, 56, 56, 56, 56, 56, 56." (entry by _Jonathan F. Waldmann_, May 26 2021). A344845 has the same inequality a(n) > sqrt(3/4)*m (conjectured), by the same author, May 29 2021.

Referees: A. Mazel, I. Stuhl, Y. Suhov, "High-density hard-core model on Z^2 and norm equations in ring Z[...]", arXiv:1909.11648 (v1 25 Sep 2019; v3 22 Jun 2023). Lemma 3.4.4, eq. (3.1): sqrt(3)D^2/2 < S(D) < sqrt(3)D^2/2 + sqrt(2)D. S(D) is twice the minimal area of non-obtuse Z^2-triangles with sides >= D, so A344710(n) = S(sqrt n). The paper calls the lower bound "obvious". D. Krachun, "Triangles on Z^2 and sliding phenomenon" / "Extreme Gibbs measures for high-density hard-core model on Z^2", arXiv:1912.07566 (Dec 2019 / Jun 2020). Definition 2.1 gives the same S(D) for all D > 0, and Theorem 2 gives S(D) = (sqrt3/2)D^2 + O(D^{4/5}). The underlying inequality is the classical one: a non-obtuse triangle with all sides >= D has area >= (sqrt3/4)D^2, since area = (1/2)ab sin C with the largest angle C in [60,90] degrees. Equality would need an equilateral lattice triangle, and Z^2 has none. OEIS A344710 and A344845 (local mirror and GitHub, revisions #84/#52 of Feb 2022) still list the inequality as conjectured.

results.title: A348484: no two squares two steps apart; the conjectured formula holds
results.summary: For every n >= 1, let a(n) be the largest number of squares you can choose on an n x n board so that no two chosen squares are exactly two steps apart in the same row or in the same column. Then a(n) = n^2/2 if n ≡ 0 (mod 4), a(n) = (n^2+1)/2 if n is odd, and a(n) = n^2/2 + 2 if n ≡ 2 (mod 4). (This is Yang Hong's conjecture in OEIS A348484.)
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: %F A348484 Conjectures: a(n) = n^2/2 for n == 0 (mod 4). a(n) = (n^2 + 1)/2 for n == 1 or 3 (mod 4). a(n) = n^2/2 + 2 for n == 2 (mod 4).  (Entry by _Yang Hong_, Oct 20 2021; last edit #33, Dec 06 2022.)

Referees: OEIS A348484 (Yang Hong, Oct 20 2021; latest revision #33, Dec 06 2022) still marks the formulas as "Conjectures". R. J. Mathar's Dec 2022 comment gives a 2×2-block checkerboard construction. Its g.f. -x(1+2x-2x^2+2x^3+x^4)/((1+x)(1+x^2)(x-1)^3) matches the conjectured values, but he states it only as a lower bound. Cross-reference: A048716 (the 1-D row condition, k AND 4k = 0). I found no published or online proof of the upper bound on arXiv, Math StackExchange, MathOverflow, SeqFan or general web search. The result does follow directly from the standard fact that a grid graph P_a□P_b has independence number ⌈ab/2⌉, because the "two apart" graph is a disjoint union of four such grids.

results.title: Even and odd legs with odd prime factors ≡ 3 (mod 4): a(n)/n → π (A354571, A354570)
results.summary: A354571 lists the even legs k of primitive Pythagorean triangles in increasing order, each repeated once per triangle. A leg is included when every odd prime factor of k is ≡ 3 (mod 4) and k has at least one odd prime factor. A354570 lists the odd legs k in the same way, for k whose prime factors are all ≡ 3 (mod 4). Selle's conjecture says that a(n)/n → π for A354571 and A354570(n)/n → π. The formal `statement` is the conjunction of these two limits, with each sequence read as the n-th term of the list where k appears #legTriangles(k) times.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: "Conjecture: lim_{n->oo} a(n)/n = Pi. Also, lim_{n->oo} A354570(n)/n = Pi." (Lothar Selle, Jun 04 2022; same text in A354570)

Referees: No prior resolution found.
- OEIS A354571 and A354570 (Lothar Selle, Jun 2022; last edited Aug 2022) still state lim a(n)/n = Pi as a conjecture. Checked in the local mirror and in upstream raw.githubusercontent.com/oeis/oeisdata.
- Selle, "Kleines Handbuch Pythagoreische Zahlentripel" (BoD 2022), ch. 2.3.10, is cited only for the equality of the two limits; I could not access the book.
- Related unproved Selle conjectures appear in A120427, A120890 and A354569.
- Web searches (arXiv, MathOverflow, Math.SE, SeqFan) found no proof or counterexample.
- The underlying asymptotic is a standard consequence of Wiener–Ikehara/Delange applied to (1-2^-s)zeta(s)/L(s,chi4), using L(1,chi4) = pi/4. D. N. Lehmer (Amer. J. Math. 22, 1900) treats similar Pythagorean counting asymptotics, but not this restricted case.

results.title: Integer partial sums of the Calkin-Wilf ratios fusc(k)/fusc(k+1) at n = 2*4^k-1 and 2*4^k-2 (A355076)
results.summary: Let fusc be Stern's diatomic sequence (fusc 0 = 0, fusc 1 = 1, fusc(2n) = fusc n, fusc(2n+1) = fusc n + fusc(n+1)), and let a(n) be the denominator of s(n) = sum_{k=0}^{n} fusc(k)/fusc(k+1). Then for every k >= 0, a(n) = 1 when n = 2*4^k - 1 or n = 2*4^k - 2. In other words, s(n) is an integer for those n.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: Conjecture: a(n) = 1 for n of the form 2*4^k - 1 or 2*4^k - 2 for some k >= 0. (entry by _Rémy Sigrist_, Jun 18 2022)

Referees: - **Row-sum theorem (the key ingredient):** K. Siddharth Choudary and A. Satyanarayana Reddy, "Calkin-Wilf tree", arXiv:2003.13466 [math.CO], Mar 2020, accepted in Resonance. Theorem 1.1, Part 11: the sum of all elements in level n (root at level 1) is 3·2^{n−2} − 1/2, proved by induction.
- **Earlier statement of the same fact:** OEIS A052940, comment by Carl Najafi (Jul 10 2011): 3·2^n − 1 is the numerator of the sum of terms at the n-th level of the Calkin-Wilf tree.
- **Classical facts:** OEIS A002487 records a(2^k) = 1 and a(2^k − 1) = k (Adamchuk comment), and that a(n)/a(n+1) enumerates the rationals (Stern; N. Calkin and H. Wilf, "Recounting the rationals", Amer. Math. Monthly 107 (2000)).
- **The conjecture itself:** OEIS A355076 (R. Sigrist, Jun 18 2022, rev. #11) is still listed as a conjecture with no %E edits. A355075 is the matching numerators entry. I found no explicit resolution anywhere; the result follows immediately from the Choudary–Reddy row sum plus the classical facts above.

results.title: A355339: the central even run of the knight-move triangle has length 1 iff n = 2^m - 2
results.summary: Let T(n,k) be the knight-move triangle A355320. It is defined by T(0,0)=1, with zero entries outside |k| <= 2n, and T(n,k) = T(n-1,k-2) + T(n-1,k+2) + T(n-2,k-1) + T(n-2,k+1). Let a(n) be the length of the maximal block of consecutive even entries of row n that contains the centre k=0. It is 0 if T(n,0) is odd, and a(0)=0. Then for every n >= 0, a(n) = 1 if and only if n > 0 and n = 2^m - 2 for some m >= 0 (equivalently, n+2 = 2^{t+2} for some t >= 0).
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: %F Conjecture: a(n) = 1 iff n > 0 and n belongs to A000918. (Rémy Sigrist, Jun 29 2022)

Referees: - OEIS A355339 (Rémy Sigrist, Jun 29 2022): the conjecture is in %F and is still unresolved at revision #10, with no %E extensions (checked in the local mirror and upstream oeisdata on GitHub).
- OEIS A355320 (the triangle; its %F gives T(n,0)=A096609(n) and T(n,1)=A096610(n), but nothing on parity).
- OEIS A096608–A096612 (Kimberling 2004, Catalan knight paths in the right half-plane), A096587, A361292, A000918, A002605: no parity results.
- J.-L. Baril, N. Hassler, S. Kirgizov, J. L. Ramírez, "Grand zigzag knight's paths", arXiv:2402.04851 (ECA 2024): its only parity remark (Remark 3.2) concerns zigzag path counts being even when n ≡ k (mod 2), not this conjecture.
- J.-L. Baril, J. L. Ramírez, "Knight's paths towards Catalan numbers", arXiv:2206.12087: nothing on parity.
- Web searches of arXiv, MathOverflow/MSE, SeqFan and general sources found no prior proof or counterexample.
- No formalization in google-deepmind formal-conjectures.

results.title: A356360: the continued-fraction denominators are 1 or prime
results.summary: For n >= 3, let a(n) be the denominator, in lowest terms, of the continued fraction 1/(2 - 3/(3 - 4/(4 - ... ((n-1) - n/(n+1))))). Then every a(n) is 1 or a prime. This is the conjecture Mohammed Bouras stated in OEIS A356360 (2022).
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: A356360: "Conjecture: The sequence contains only 1's and the primes." (_Mohammed Bouras_, Oct 15 2022). The same sentence appears in A369797 (Feb 2024), A370726 (Feb 2024) and A372763 ('Conjecture 1', May 2024). A372761: "Conjecture 1: Except for 4, the sequence contains only 1's and the primes." A362086: "Conjecture: Except for 9, every term of this sequence is either a prime or 1." A363482: "Conjecture: Except for 49, every term of this sequence is either a prime or 1." (all by Bouras)

Referees: OEIS A356360 (mirror 2026-10-17, rev #31 Aug 2024): still marked "Conjecture". It has an unproved comment "Same as A128059(n), A145737(n-1), A097302(n-2) for n>5", and its formula "a(n)=2n-1 if prime else 1 (n != 5)" is labeled "From the conjecture". M. Bouras, "The Distribution Of Prime Numbers And The Continued Fractions", Zenodo doi:10.5281/zenodo.7212512 (2022; also viXra 2209.0101): proves only the closed form (Thm 1.1) and states Conjecture 3.1, verified to n=10000. M. Bouras, "A New Primes-Generating Sequence", arXiv:2509.09745 (2025), Table 2 (k=1 row = A356360): observation only, no proof. Bouras slides, Zenodo 10992128: "Conjecture 2", no proof. AlphaProof Nexus results / formal-conjectures auto_oeis THEOREM_MAPPING and T. Adamczewski, "OEIS Open", arXiv:2608.11941: A356360 is not included; only the sibling A372761 Conj. 2 was resolved. Related but distinct: A356247 conjectures proved by B. Cloitre (2025, OEIS attachment). No prior proof or counterexample found.

results.title: Internal n-gons in a regular n-gon: triple points occur only for n = 3, 4, 6, and otherwise there are n k^2 + 1 regions (Shannon's A357216 conjecture)
results.summary:
Take the regular n-gon with vertices V_j = exp(2πij/n). Divide each side into k+1 equal parts. For m = 1..k, the m-th internal n-gon joins the m-th division points of consecutive sides. Its side (j, m-1) is the segment from the m-th division point of side j to the m-th division point of side j+1. The statement has two parts.
(1) For n >= 3, some k gives a point lying on three distinct drawn sides if and only if n is 3, 4 or 6.
(2) For n = 5 and for every n >= 7 and every k >= 0, the open polygon minus all n*k drawn sides has exactly n*k^2 + 1 connected components.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: %C Conjecture: the only n-gons that contain non-simple intersections are the 3-gon (triangle), 4-gon (square), and 6-gon (hexagon). %F Conjectured formula for all columns for n >= 7: T(n,k) = n*k^2 + 1. %F Conjectured formula for all rows except for n = 3, 4, 6: T(n,k) = n*k^2 + 1. (Scott R. Shannon, Sep 18 2022; the same conjecture appears in A357235 (vertices n*k^2+n) and A357254 (edges 2n*k^2+n))

Referees: I found no prior resolution. The OEIS entries A357216, A357235 and A357254 (Scott R. Shannon, Sep 2022, last revised Sep 21 2022, no %E lines) still list both claims as conjectures, in the local mirror and the current GitHub oeisdata. The related entries for the triangle (A356984, with Talmon Silver's classification for n = 3 only), the square (A357058) and the hexagon (A357196) give no general proof. arXiv API searches for "A357216" and "internal n-gons" returned nothing. Web searches covering MathOverflow, Math StackExchange, SeqFan and Google-Scholar-style queries found only the OEIS entries themselves. Sela Fried, "Proofs of some Conjectures from the OEIS" (arXiv:2410.07237) is unrelated. The key tool, Niven's theorem (cos(2*pi/n) is rational only for n = 1, 2, 3, 4, 6), is classical.

results.title: OEIS A362086: every denominator of 1/(2-3/(3-4/(...(n-1)-n/(-3)))) except 9 is 1 or a prime

results.title: OEIS A363482: apart from 49, every denominator of 1/(2-3/(3-4/(...(n-1)-n/(-5)))) is 1 or a prime
results.summary: For n >= 3 let t_n = -5 and t_k = k - (k+1)/t_{k+1} for k = n-1, ..., 2. Let a(n) be the denominator, in lowest terms, of 1/t_2 = 1/(2-3/(3-4/(...(n-1)-n/(-5)))). results.title: A363609: a(k^3) = 6k(k+2), the cube is the optimal polycube of k^3 dice
results.summary: Each standard die has opposite faces summing to 7, all dice have the same chirality, and each die may take any of its 24 rotations. Build a face-connected polycube from n dice. A face is visible when the neighbouring cell is empty; faces underneath and faces facing an internal cavity also count. a(n) is the least possible number of visible pips. Claim: for every k > 1, a(k^3) = 6(k+2)k.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: %F A363609 Conjecture: a(k^3) = 6*(k+2)*k for k > 1.  (Unattributed formula line. Entry by _Matt Donahoe_, Jun 11 2023; last edit #45, Sep 03 2023.)

Referees: I found no prior resolution.
- OEIS A363609, by Matt Donahoe, Jun 11 2023 (revision #45, Sep 03 2023): the local mirror is identical to oeis/oeisdata main on GitHub, and it still states the formula as "Conjecture: a(k^3) = 6*(k+2)*k for k > 1".
- Michael S. Branicky's formulas in the same entry, Jun 11 and Jun 15 2023: these give only upper bounds and loose bounds.
- Donahoe's program, https://github.com/mdonahoe/oeis/blob/main/A363609/dice.py, with its out.txt: a heuristic search over box-plus-slab layouts, with no optimality proof.
- OEIS A193416, minimum surface area of polycubes: the unweighted analogue, a(n^3) = 6n^2.
- AMC 10A 2002 Problem 18 (https://artofproblemsolving.com/wiki/index.php/2002_AMC_10A_Problems/Problem_18): computes the minimum for the 3x3x3 cube alone, 90. It does not show that the cube is optimal among all polycubes.
- Loomis and Whitney, Bull. AMS 55 (1949) 961-962: the classical inequality behind the projection step.

results.title: Edges of the all-chords graph of a triangle with n general-position points per side (A367119)
results.summary: Take the equilateral triangle with corners 0, 1 and 1/2 + (√3/2)i. Let B be the three corners together with exactly n points in the relative interior of each side, and no other points. Draw the segment between every pair of distinct points of B; pairs on a common side give pieces of that side. Assume general position: no interior point of the triangle lies on three pairwise distinct drawn segments. Form the planar graph whose vertices are the points of B together with every point where two drawn segments meet in a single point. Two distinct vertices are adjacent when they lie on a common drawn segment and no vertex lies strictly between them. Then for every n ≥ 0 this graph has (3/2)(3n^4 + 4n^3 + 3n^2 + 4n + 2) edges. This was conjectured by Shannon and Sloane for OEIS A367119.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: %F Conjecture: a(n) = (3/2)*(3*n^4 + 4*n^3 + 3*n^2 + 4*n + 2). (Scott R. Shannon and N. J. A. Sloane, Nov 05 2023)

Referees: OEIS sources (read from the local mirror and checked against GitHub oeisdata main):
- A367119 (Shannon and Sloane, Nov 05 2023): the edge formula is still marked "Conjecture"; last edited Nov 09 2023.
- A367117: "Theorem: a(n) = (3/4)*(n+1)*(3*n^3+n^2+4)" for the vertex count of the same configuration. This is the key prior result, since the edge formula follows from it by degree counting: E = 2V + 3(n^2−1).
- A213827: "a(n) = (A367177 [sic, i.e. A367117](n) − 3*(n+1))/3 – Shannon & Sloane, Nov 09 2023". This is the interior-crossing count n^2(n+1)(3n+1)/4 per side-orbit.
- A367183 (Nov 13 2023): T(3,k) = A367117(k) appears apart from its "Conjectured" rows.
- A365929: Sloane's proof (Nov 07 2023) of the crossing count for the corner-free triangle variant.
- A366932 and A367015: the analogous edge and region conjectures, marked "now a theorem" by Sloane on Dec 31 2025.
- A392261, A392282, A392228 (Shannon and Sloane, Jan 2026): Shannon's attached proof (a392261.txt) of the general vertex, edge and region formulas for k general points per side of a regular n-gon without corners. The local mirror holds only a git-lfs pointer and the file could not be fetched; oeis.org was not queried, as instructed.
- A367190 and A366253: the triangle row (n=3) with corners is listed as a conjecture.

Web searches (arXiv, Math StackExchange, general) found no paper or post that explicitly proves the A367119 or A367118 conjecture. The general method is the classical Euler-formula and crossing-count argument for chord arrangements (Moser's circle problem; Poonen–Rubinstein, arXiv math/9508209).

results.title: The least number of inequivalent cells of a (6k+5)-iamond is 3(k+1)
results.summary: For every k >= 0, the least number of inequivalent cells over all polyiamonds with n = 6k+5 cells is 3(k+1). Two cells of P are equivalent when a symmetry of the triangular grid maps P onto itself and one cell to the other. This is Exley's conjecture in OEIS A369366, a(6k+5) = 3(k+1).
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: %C A369366 Conjecture: a(6k+5) = 3(k+1) for all k >= 0. Observed for k = 0, 1, 2 (n = 5, 11, 17). The next test case is a(23), predicted to be 12.  (From _Peter Exley_, Apr 07 2026)

Referees: OEIS A369366 (local mirror revision #14, Apr 14 2026, identical to oeisdata main): Exley's comment of Apr 07 2026 states the conjecture and already proves the lower bound a(6k+5) >= 3(k+1) (no rotations are possible when n = 6k+5, so |G_max| = 2). No upper-bound construction or full proof appears in the entry or its %E history. Cross-references checked: A369365, A369367, A369363, A369364, A367758, A367759, A373637, A376798, A376799. The only related proof is Mason and von Brömssen's formula proof for the polyomino analog A367758 (square lattice, a different problem). Exley's linked GitHub repo github.com/pexley-math/oeis-A369366 and the account page return 404 and could not be inspected. Web searches (arXiv, general web) found no prior resolution.

results.title: A375522: S2(n) - S1(n) = 1 fails at n = 42 (the difference is 5)
results.summary: Let p_k be the k-th prime. Define s(0) = 0 and s(k) = s(k-1) + 1/(p_k b(k)), where b(k) = 1 + floor(1/((1 - s(k-1)) p_k)) (this is A375781). Write s(n) = S1(n)/S2(n) in lowest terms (S2 = A375522, S1 = A375521). Sigrist and Sloane conjectured that S2(n) - S1(n) = 1 for every n >= 1 except n = 4 and n = 6. This is false: S2(42) - S1(42) = 5. Lean: theorem result : ¬ statement.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: The differences S2(n) - S1(n) are surprisingly small: for n = 1,2,...,34 the values S2(n) - S1(n) are: 1, 1, 1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 1, ..., 1 suggesting the conjecture that they are always 1 except for n = 4 and 6 (compare the Theorem in A374983). (Rémy Sigrist and N. J. A. Sloane, Aug 30 2024)

Referees: The conjecture is in OEIS A375522 (R. Sigrist and N. J. A. Sloane, Aug 30 2024; comment added Aug 31 2024; current revision #25, Apr 22 2025). It is restated as still open ("it seems") in A375528 (Sloane, Sep/Oct 2024). Related: A375521, A375781, A374983/A375516 (harmonic analogue, proved by Sigrist), and Sloane, "A Nasty Surprise in a Sequence and Other OEIS Stories", Rutgers Experimental Math Seminar, Oct 10 2024 (slides list these sequences and a general Conjecture 4, with no counterexample). Sigrist and Sloane, "Dampening Down a Divergent Series", is still cited on OEIS as a manuscript in preparation. No prior counterexample or proof turned up in the OEIS histories, arXiv (e.g. Fried arXiv:2607.24832 does not cover it), web searches, or google-deepmind/formal-conjectures. The SeqFan archive could not be reached.

results.title: A386538: moving the circle's center off the grid enlarges the max lattice polygon (counterexample at n = 7)
results.summary: Conjecture (OEIS A386538, Felix Huber): for every n ≥ 0, the largest area of a polygon with vertices on Z^2 inside the closed disk of radius n is the same whether the disk's center is a grid point or any point of the plane. In the frozen encoding: for all n : ℕ, ⨆_{c ∈ ℝ²} vol(conv(Z² ∩ B(c, n))) = vol(conv(Z² ∩ B(0, n))). We prove the negation. At n = 7 with center c0 = (5/12, 5/24), the convex hull of the lattice points in B(c0, 7) has area at least 277/2 = 138.5. The convex hull for the center 0 has area at most 3457/25 = 138.28; its true value is 138 = a(7).
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: "Conjecture: The maximum possible area of a polygon within the circle would be the same if only the vertices but not the center were fixed on grid points." (entry by _Felix Huber_, Aug 05 2025). The same conjecture appears for ellipses in A386539, which has T(n,n) = A386538(n).

Referees: Sources checked:
- Local OEIS mirror and raw.githubusercontent.com/oeis/oeisdata, A386538: #23, Aug 19 2025, no %E lines. A386539: #19, Aug 19 2025.
- Entries that cite A386538/A386539: A398490, A396223, A391113. None addresses the conjecture.
- Cross-references read: A066643, A123690, A125228, A288247, A322106, A322107, A357577, A108126. None resolves it. A123690 and A295344 concern lattice-point counts with an off-grid center, not polygon areas.
- Web searches for the A386538 number, the entry's wording, Felix Huber plus counterexample, SeqFan, and MathOverflow/Math.SE on convex hulls of lattice points in a shifted disk.

Related but not resolving:

results.title: No primitive Heronian triangle has integer circumradius
results.summary: Let x, y, z be positive integers satisfying the strict triangle inequalities, with gcd(x, y, z) = 1, and let K be a natural number with 16K^2 = (x+y+z)(-x+y+z)(x-y+z)(x+y-z), i.e. K is the area. Then there is no natural number R with 4KR = xyz. In other words, no primitive Heronian triangle has integer circumradius. This is Felix Huber's conjecture in OEIS A392943.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: "Conjecture: There is no primitive Heronian triangle with integer circumradius." (entry by _Felix Huber_, Feb 04 2026)

Referees: Ronald van Luijk, "The diameter of the circumcircle of a Heron triangle", Elemente der Mathematik 63 (2008), 118–121. The relevant parts are:
- Theorem 2, (4)⇒(5): if gcd(a,b,c,d) = 1, every prime divisor of the circumdiameter d is ≡ 1 mod 4.
- Corollary 5: for a prime p ≢ 1 mod 4, p^{v_p(d)} divides gcd(a,b,c).
- Proof of Theorem 1: it states explicitly that a Heron triangle with integer circumradius has all sides even.

Earlier related work:
- A.-V. Kramer & F. Luca, "Some remarks on Heron triangles", Acta Acad. Paedagog. Agriensis Sect. Mat. (N.S.) 27 (2000) 25–38. Shows no power of 2 is the circumradius of a Heron triangle.
- M. Aassila, "Some results on Heron triangles", Elem. Math. 56 (2001) 143–146.

Also related, with full text not checked: E. Read, "Integer triangles with integer circumradii", Math. Gazette 107 (2023) 241–248.

OEIS A392943 (Huber, Feb 2026) cites none of these, and no proof has been added to the entry.

results.title: The 1089-trick map has two 9-digit fixed points (A393794 uniqueness conjecture is false)
results.summary: Let rev(m) be the decimal reversal of m (leading zeros dropped), and let T(x) = D + rev(D) with D = |x - rev(x)|. Havenaar's conjecture in A393794 says that for every n >= 1, a(n) = 110*(10^(n+1) - 1) is the only fixed point of T with exactly n+4 decimal digits. This is false. For n = 5, x = 108910890 has 9 digits and satisfies T(x) = x, but x is not a(5) = 109999890.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: "a(n) is the unique fixed point of the 1089-trick map T among all (n+4)-digit numbers (verified exhaustively for n = 1..4; conjectured for all n >= 1)." results.title: Bar tilings of the smallest-perimeter rectangle: a(n+1) = 4 a(n) for odd n >= 3 (A394981)
results.summary: Let a(n) be the number of tilings, counted up to the symmetries of the rectangle, of the rows(n) x cols(n) rectangle by the n bars 1x1, 1x2, ..., 1xn, each used exactly once. Here rows(n) = floor((n+1)/2) and cols(n) = (n(n+1)/2)/rows(n). For n = 2m+1 the rectangle is (m+1) x (2m+1), and for n = 2m+2 it is (m+1) x (2m+3). In Lean, a(n) is the frozen bitmask-search definition: it sums the stabilizer sizes of all tilings found by the search and divides by the order of the symmetry group (Burnside). Claim (A394981 conjecture, read for odd n >= 3): for every odd n >= 3, a(n+1) = 4 a(n). The literal case n = 1 fails, a(2) = 1 != 4 = 4 a(1), and the statement excludes it.
results.notes:

results.title: A397315: a 14-point blackout of the 5 x 8 grid refutes T(n,m) = n + m
results.summary: Pemmasani's conjecture in OEIS A397315 says this. Let T(n,k) be the largest number of points that can be blacked out of the grid {0..k-1} x {0..n-1} so that every lattice rectangle (tilted rectangles included) is still determined by its set of visible vertices. Then T(n,m) = n + m whenever min(n,m) >= 4, except T(4,4) = 7 and T(4,5) = T(5,4) = 8. We prove the negation. The 5 x 8 grid (n = 5, k = 8) has a valid blackout of 14 points, so T(5,8) >= 14, which is more than the predicted 5 + 8 = 13.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: "Conjecture: T(n,m) = n+m whenever min(n,m) >= 4, except T(4,4) = 7 and T(4,5) = 8 (verified on seven cells through 6 X 6)." (entry by _Arjun Pemmasani_, Sep 02 2026; comment in the entry, which was last revised Sep 12 2026)

results.title: No odd n with a(n) > 1 has b^n ≡ b^{a(n)} (mod n) for all b (OEIS A051903)
results.summary: Let a(n) be the largest exponent in the prime factorization of n (OEIS A051903; a(1) = 0). Thomas Ordowski (Dec 2019) asked: are there odd numbers n with a(n) > 1 and b^n ≡ b^{a(n)} (mod n) for every natural number b? The upstream formal statement says such an n exists. We prove its negation: there is no odd n with a(n) > 1 such that b^n ≡ b^{a(n)} (mod n) for all b ∈ ℕ.

results.title: An odd n with a(n) > 1 and 2^n ≡ 2^{a(n)} (mod n), where a(n) is the largest prime exponent of n (OEIS A051903, Ordowski)
